extracted.intended_audience: readers and analysts of Rabelaisian satire and comic technique (humor scholars, writers studying grotesque/scatological comedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and label the distinct comic devices, narrative strategies, and satirical targets exemplified in this chunk of Rabelais' Gargantua. Focus is on the techniques a writer or critic could use to produce or evaluate similar humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque exaggeration / hyperbole
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of enormous scale and extravagant comparisons (e.g., the mare 'as big as six elephants', tails 'little more or less than every whit as great as the steeple-pillar of St. Mark').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ extreme, disproportionate images to create astonishment and comic shock; escalate details (size, weight, number) to absurdity. Example in text: the mare's foot- and tail-descriptions and the Scythian rams anecdote. Anti-pattern: overuse without variation can flatten the effect; maintain specific vivid details to keep the image entertaining rather than tedious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scatological / bodily-detail humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended focus on excrement, wiping, and other 'base' bodily acts (the long torchecul/wipebreech catalogue, songs and rhymes about 'shitting', 'wipe my bum', descriptions of methods and sensations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground humor in frank, sensory bodily detail for shock, intimacy, and earthy comic truth; use inventive vocabulary and surprising analogies (e.g., 'the neck of a goose... temporate heat... comes even to the regions of the heart and brains'). Anti-pattern: gratuitous nastiness without wit or variation can alienate readers—Rabelais balances scatology with lyricism and learned parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-heroic inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating trivial or vulgar actions with grand, epic language or social ceremony (e.g., treating wiping, gifts of a mare, or taking bells as matters warranting oration and ceremony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast high register and ceremonial treatment with low subject-matter to generate irony and parody. Example: Janotus' 'oration' for the bells and the full-hall procession to request their return for what are essentially petty civic problems. Anti-pattern: if the register and subject are not sufficiently at odds, the inversion loses its comic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody of learned/scholastic language and pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation and deformation of academic/Latin-scholastic speech into gibberish and pseudo-authoritative jargon (Janotus' speech full of Latin tags, mock-logical jargon, and invented declensions: 'Omnis bella bellabilis...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimic the rhythms, citations, and formal markers of erudition while corrupting them into absurdity to lampoon pedantry. Use false authorities, mock citations, and Latinized nonsense. Example: Janotus' mixture of Latin, French, and comic non sequiturs. Anti-pattern: mere gibberish without recognizable markers of the target register will not read as parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neologisms, playful coinages and compound insults
rubrics_metrics.description: Invented compound words and grotesque coinages that compress insult, device-name, or mock-technicality (e.g., 'torchecul', 'wipe-breech', 'arsewisps', 'bumfodders', 'merdi', 'gudgeron' style terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coin vivid new words to capture comic objects/concepts and to characterize speakers or practices. Neologisms can localize humor, produce surprise, and embed social commentary. Example: long lists of alternative torcheculs with novel names. Anti-pattern: opaque coinages that readers cannot parse will block the joke—anchor invented words with context or analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative catalogue / list-accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Long, piling lists of items (books read, wiping materials, tail-descriptions, garments) that accumulate absurdity by repetition and variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use enumerations to build momentum: each successive item should add a new twist or escalate the absurdity. Examples: Gargantua's long litany of wipe-substitutes and the exhaustive list of authors/readings. Anti-pattern: lists that repeat without invention become monotonous rather than funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inserted comic songs, rhymes and rounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Short comic poems or roundelays embedded in the prose (e.g., the rude rhyme and 'A Roundelay' about 'shitting yes’day' and the skiter-song).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break narrative flow with lyrical or metrical bursts to vary pacing and add performative, chant-like humor. Songs can crystallize jokes (mnemonic, catchy) and present obscene material in a playful form. Anti-pattern: poorly metrical or tonally inconsistent verses can disrupt rather than amuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character contrast and naïf-wise protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a seemingly naive or child figure (Gargantua) whose utterances reveal surprising worldly wit and authoritative opinion (e.g., his confident claim about the goose-neck as the best wipe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create comedic tension by attributing subversive knowledge or worldly confidence to an unexpected social type (child, bumpkin). The contrast between apparent innocence and bold pronouncement magnifies the joke. Anti-pattern: if the character lacks consistent grounding, the contrast can feel arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical slapstick and visual gag description
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of brute physical action for comic effect (the mare 'unsheathed her tail' and felled the wood, the drawing of Gargantua's mentul and the piss-flood on Parisians, the lever dropping under stairs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage large, visible actions with clear cause-and-effect and sensory detail to create a comedic spectacle. Use concrete verbs and consequential images (floods, sweeping, crashing). Anti-pattern: vagueness or lack of consequence reduces visual comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire of institutions and professions
rubrics_metrics.description: Targeting universities, legal courts, sophisters, and civic bodies for ridicule (e.g., mockery of the faculty, suits in law described as interminable, the orator who will be paid in sausages and breeches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose pretension and hypocrisy by showing institutional rituals as self-serving, silly, or corrupt. Use concrete scenes (an oration, a law-suit, vows to stop snuffing noses) to exemplify broader institutional folly. Anti-pattern: satire without specific, recognizable behaviors risks vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony, faux-earnest praise and mock solemnity
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious-sounding praise and solemn formulas applied to ridiculous ends (e.g., 'a pair of breeches is good, et vir sapiens non abhorrebit eam' delivered as a grave motive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an earnest voice to praise trivialities or to lend mock gravity to base motives; this heightens irony. Keep rhetorical markers of sincerity (blessings, invocations) to sharpen the contrast. Anti-pattern: if the sincere tone is too obviously ludicrous, the irony can flatten into mere silliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilingual code-switching and phonetic comic mimicry
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing Latin, French, vernacular, and phonetic onomatopoeic gibberish to comic effect (Janotus alternates Latin tags, French phrases, and comic noises: 'Hem, hem, gud-day, sirs... Reddite quae sunt Caesaris... Hem, hashchehhawksash').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switch registers and languages to create comic incongruity and to mock pretension; phonetic renderings emphasize character and social milieu. Use recognizable fragments of learned language so the parody reads. Anti-pattern: inaccessible polyglossia will lose readers who don't catch the references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running gags and ironic deferment
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurrence of promises/vows and chronically deferred outcomes for comic payoff (e.g., the court's decree to be given at the 'next Greek kalends, that is, never').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce a motif or promise and repeatedly defer or subvert it to produce cumulative irony. The 'never' payoff becomes an expected comic result. Anti-pattern: if the running gag is not revisited or lacks variation, it fails to accumulate humor.
